newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Turkish premier offers to boost trade with Libya.
newsitem.headline: Turkish premier offers to boost trade with Libya.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, on a controversial visit to Libya, has met Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and offered to triple trade with the north African country if it pays it debts.

The official Libyan news agency JANA said on Sunday that the meeting with Gaddafi was held on Saturday in the Libyan coastal city of Sirte, some 450 km (250 miles) east of Tripoli. It gave no details of the discussions.

Earlier Turkey's state-run Anatolian agency quoted Erbakan as telling his hosts that Turkey could boost trade with Libya. "It was decided that the trade volume with Libya will be raised to $2 billion." he was quoted as saying.

Speaking after meeting his Libyan counterpart Abdelmajid al Su'ud on Saturday, Erbakan said the condition for increasing trade was Libya's repayment of more than $300 million due to Turkish contractors.

To reach Libya Erbakan flew from Cairo to the Tunisian island of Jerba and then travelled by road across the border, a Turkish diplomat in Tunis said. He could not fly to Tripoli because of U.N. sanctions imposed on Libya for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over Scotland in 1988.

Turkey's Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, the Islamists' conservative coalition partner, has described the visit as ill-timed while the interior minister, a member of Ciller's party, has threatened to resign over the trip. Ciller herself visited Libya and met Gaddafi in 1994, when she was prime minister.
Washington, already wary of modern Turkey's first Islamist leader -- who made a state visit to Iran over the summer after taking office -- has expressed disquiet at the Libya visit.

The United States accuses both Libya and Iran of sponsoring state terrorism and has rebuked its NATO ally for forging closer ties with the two countries. Few foreign leaders have visited Tripoli since the United Nations imposed an air and limited trade embargo on Libya.
But Erbakan has said that the visit was necessary for Turkey's commercial interests.
Bilateral trade between Libya and Turkey in 1995 rose to $623 million from $498 million.
Anatolian news agency has quoted Erbakan as saying Libya could sell Turkey oil, natural gas, petrochemicals and fertiliser and buy food, textiles and industrial products.
Erbakan is due to travel on Sunday from Libya to Nigeria, also rich in natural resources but under fire from the West over the human rights record of its military government.
